Define each feature with entity keys, transformation version, event time, availability/ingestion time, and freshness requirements. Keep an immutable offline history and materialize the latest valid values into an online key-value store. For training, retrieve only data that would have been available at prediction time; event-time filtering alone can leak a late-arriving record that was not yet known.

Share transformation definitions between batch and streaming paths and validate them with replay/parity tests. Materialization should be idempotent and reject older updates that arrive after newer ones. Include feature versions in model dependencies, and deploy compatible model/feature revisions together. Online requests need bounded timeouts, freshness metadata, and defined defaults for absent values.

No architecture guarantees literally zero train-serve skew. Measure value discrepancies, missingness, lateness, and transformation drift; replay logged serving inputs to diagnose failures. Partition online keys by entity, monitor hot keys, and backfill offline history without silently rewriting serving state. The tradeoff is fast current lookups versus faithful historical reconstruction; one store rarely serves both workloads equally well.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** A point-in-time join must respect both event time and when the information became available. Formally a training feature at prediction time t may use only records available by t under the production contract. Replay sampled online requests against offline reconstruction and measure discrepancy distributions, rather than assuming shared feature names imply identical values.
